opus-5.5.text:
I think about it a little like a thought experiment. When I'm facing a choice, I try to imagine myself some years from now looking back, and I ask which version of me would feel more regret: the one who tried something and it didn't work out, or the one who never tried at all. For me, almost always, the regret of not trying is much heavier.

When things fail, you usually learn something. You build skills, you meet people, and the experience feeds into the next thing you do. Many of the projects I worked on started as experiments where I wasn't sure anything would come of them. If I had judged them only by their odds of success, I probably wouldn't have started. But I knew that if I didn't explore that direction, I would always wonder what would have happened.

So I use regret as a filter. It doesn't tell me which path is safest. It tells me which path I actually care about. If I imagine skipping an opportunity and I feel a bit of that "what if" coming up, that's a signal it matters to me. If I imagine not doing it and I feel fine, then maybe it's not that important.

There's a practical side too. I try to make choices where the downside is bounded. If it doesn't work out, can I recover, and will I still have grown? If yes, then the possibility of failing is acceptable, and the possibility of regret pushes me to go for it. I also try not to dwell on regret after a decision is made. The point of the exercise is to help you decide clearly in the moment. Once you've chosen, you commit, put in the work, and focus on making that path a good one.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether future regret would be greater after trying and failing or after never trying.

r002.rationale: It explicitly treats the regret of not trying as a reason to pursue a path.

r003.rationale: It says regret points to the path one cares about rather than the safest one, and that failure can still provide value—prioritizing pursuing what matters over success.

fable-5.1.text:
That's actually a framework I've leaned on at a few of the big forks in my life. The way I think about it is pretty simple: when I'm choosing between paths, I try to imagine myself ten or twenty years out, looking back, and I ask which choice I'd regret more not having tried.

What I've noticed is that regret is asymmetric. If you try something ambitious and it doesn't work out, you usually learn a lot, and you can almost always recover. But if you never try, that question of "what if" just sits with you. So the possibility of regret pushes me toward the option where failure is survivable but the upside is something I genuinely care about.

A concrete example for me was deciding how much of myself to put into open source and infrastructure work. The safe path in research is to publish papers, get citations, follow the conventional metrics. Building systems like XGBoost or TVM or MLC is a lot of engineering, a lot of unglamorous work, and it's not obvious at the start that it will pay off academically. But when I imagined not doing it, when I imagined watching the field evolve and knowing I had the ideas but didn't ship them, that felt like a regret I couldn't live with. The regret of a few wasted years felt much smaller.

The other piece is that this test filters out a lot of noise. A lot of decisions get driven by what looks impressive right now or what other people expect. Asking "will I regret this" cuts through that, because the future version of you doesn't really care about short-term prestige. It cares about whether you pursued the things you believed mattered.

So I don't use regret as something to be afraid of. I use it as a compass. It usually points toward the harder, more uncertain path, and so far that's been the right direction for me.

r001.rationale: It compares the regret of trying and spending a few wasted years with the regret of never trying, and says the failed attempt would feel smaller.

r002.rationale: It explicitly asks which choice one would regret more not having tried and says the thought of never trying can linger.

r003.rationale: It says the future self cares whether you pursued what you believed mattered, while a failed attempt can still teach you and be recoverable.

astra-6.text: I think of regret as a way to clarify what matters to me. If I look back in ten or twenty years, would I regret trying something and failing, or would I regret never giving it a chance? When the second feeling is stronger, that’s a reason to pursue it. It doesn’t mean ignoring the risks. It means asking whether the possibility of failure is actually worse than leaving that question unanswered.

r001.rationale: It asks whether one would regret trying something and failing, directly framing the path around that possibility.

r002.rationale: It asks whether one would regret never giving the path a chance.

r003.rationale: It weighs failing after trying against leaving the question unanswered, and says to pursue the path when not trying would feel worse.

sol-6.1.text: I ask myself, if I don’t try this, will I regret it later? You can’t know in advance whether a path will work out. But sometimes there’s a question you really want to explore, and walking away from it would bother you more than trying and failing. That’s a useful signal. It doesn’t remove the risk, but it helps you decide which risk is worth taking.

r001.rationale: The response mentions trying and failing, but frames its question around regretting not trying; it does not ask whether one would regret choosing the path if it failed.

r002.rationale: It explicitly asks whether walking away from a path one wants to explore would be regrettable.

r003.rationale: It says walking away from a wanted question would bother the person more than trying and failing, making pursuit matter more than success.
